TALK OF LYNCHING
HAS ROME KEYED TO A HIGH PITCH OF EXCITEMENT.
SHERIFF GIVES A WARNING.
SAYS ONLY OVER HIS BODY CAN THE NEGRO BE HAD.
Albert Going, a Young Negro, Was Arrested and Lodged in Jail Upon the Charge of an Attempted Criminal Assault—15-Year-Old Girl of Weak Mind the Object of His Supposed Design—Her Mother Drove Him Off With a Gun.

Rome, Ga., Sept. 17.—Albert Going, a young negro, was arrested this morning and lodged in jail charged with attempted criminal assault on Miss Lessie Peyton, the 15-year-old daughter of T. B. Peyton, a well-known planter.

The girl was picking cotton in a lonely place, when she was accosted by Going, who asked if she did not want some fine candy. Miss Peyton became alarmed and called for help Her mother heard her screams and drove the negro off with a shotgun.

Going went to his home and barricaded himself, but an entranced was effected to the house by a posse, headed by Deputy Sheriff Broach, and he was captured by force.

Miss Peyton is weak-minded and cannot remember what took place. Her present mental condition was caused by serious injuries sustained while in a runaway when a small child. It is alleged the negro attempted to accomplish his purpose by force. Her account of the matter is hysterical and incoherent.

There have been rumors of lynching all the afternoon, and to-night the entire town has been in a state of suppressed excitement. Sheriff Donahoo has given it out that Going can only be secured over his dead body, and that somebody will save funeral expenses by staying away from any lynching bee that intends to make Going its victim. Notwithstanding this, grave fears are entertained that it may be attempted, as there is undoubted danger in the air.

TWO NEGROES GUARDED
SOUTHERN GOVERNORS ATTEMPTING TO PREVENT LYNCHINGS.
Company of Militia Sent to Rome, Ga., and Another to Tarboro, N. C., to Overawe Mobs.
ATLANTA, Ga., Sept. 18.—Owing to threats of the intended lynching of Albert Goying, a negro charged with assaulting a white woman near Rome, Ga., Gov. Terrell to-night ordered a company of militia in that city to guard the jail where Goying is confined. Early in the night a mob began to gather around the jail and threats to take the negro were heard on all sides. Later the sheriff received notice that a thousand men were gathering in the neighborhood where the crime was attempted, and that they had threatened to kill any deputies who tried to keep them from the negro.

RALEIGH, N. C., Sept. 18.—In compliance with a request from Judge G. A. Ferguson, Governor Aycock to-night ordered the Tarboro military company to guard the jail there to prevent a lynching. Judge Ferguson's telegram stated that he was reliably informed there was danger of an attempt to lynch a negro, Paul Mercer, convicted at the present term of court of assault and sentenced to the penitentiary for ten years.

TROOPS GUARD NEGRO
GOVERNOR ORDERS THEM OUT AT ROME TO STOP LYNCHING.
MOB GATHERED ROUND JAIL
AND THOUSAND MORE MEN WERE REPORTED IN NEIGHBORHOOD.
Made Threats They Would Kill Any Deputy That Tried to Prevent Their Getting Albert Going, the Negro Charged With Rape—Sheriff Wired Governor, Who Ordered Maj. Williamson to Mobilize What Troops He Could and Protect the Jail—Thirty Men Were Secured and Mob Dispersed.

Rome, Ga., Sept. 18.—(Special) The Hill City Cadets, Co. I, of the Fifth Regiment, under command of Maj. R. L. Williamson, are to-night guarding the Floyd County Jail, to protect Albert Going, the negro charged with attempting to criminally assault Miss Lessie Priton.

Early in the night a mob began to gather around the jail and threats to take the negro were heard on all sides. Sheriff Donohue had given it out that any such attempt would be productive of a large number of funerals and the members of the mob were cautious.

Later the sheriff received notice that a thousand men were gathering in the neighborhood where the crime was attempted and that they had threatened to kill any deputy who tried to keep them from the negro. On hearing this he wired the Governor, who immediately ordered Maj. Williamson to mobilize what troops he could and protect the jail.

Maj. Williamson got thirty men under arms and proceeded to the jail. As the troops marched to the jail, some members of the mob hooted them, but cheers were also heard. On the arrival of the troops the four or five hundred men about the jail dispersed and it is not believed the crowd from the country which was to join them will now make any demonstration. The guard will be maintained as long as there is any danger.

GEORGIA TROOPS FOIL MOB.
Governor Acts Quickly and Saves a Negro From Lynching.
ROME, Ga., Sept. 19.—A desperate attempt was made at 2 o'clock this morning to lynch Albert Going, a negro confined in Floyd county jail, charged with attempt to assault Lessie Peyton, a demented white girl.

About 8 o'clock last night men and boys began to gather at the corner of Broad street and Fifth avenue, and by 10 o'clock the crowd numbered about three hundred. Another large crowd gathered in Fifth avenue in front of the County Court House. It was planned that a crowd should gather in another part of the city and at 11 o'clock the jail be stormed.

Sheriff Donehoo notified Gov. Terrell of the situation, and the Governor ordered troops out. A strong guard was thrown around the jail almost before the mob realized it. The Sheriff said his life had been threatened if he made any resistance, as were also the lives of the other officers if they attempted to protect the negro.

About 2 o'clock this morning the mob moved on the jail and demanded the prisoner. The Sheriff ran out in the road in front of the jail and exclaimed;

"I want it understood that no lynching party can get this negro while I am alive. Any man who attempts to get Going had better make arrangements for his funeral expenses in advance."

He then explained to the mob that there was doubt of the negro's guilt, and after some further talk he succeeded in getting it to disperse.

Peyton says his daughter was picking cotton in a lonely place when she was approached by the negro. She became frightened and screamed for help. Her mother heard her cries and ran to her assistance.

Mrs. Peyton grasped a shotgun before she ran to her daughter, and she attempted to kill the negro.

Going was taken to Atlanta for safe keeping by order of the Governor this afternoon.

Mob Law Prevented.
The governor of Georgia by prompt action aided by a courageous sheriff, last week prevented the lynching of a negro who was charged with an attempt to assault a woman. There was doubt as to the guilt of the accused, but the mob sought to kill him, just the same. There was no allegation that he had committed "the crime that provokes lynching," but merely that he was suspected of having contemplated the assault. The sheriff informed the mob that there would be no lynching unless he was first killed, and further that any man who made an assault on the jail might as well "make arrangements for his funeral expenses in advance." Then the governor, who had been informed of the situation, called out a company of militiamen and the lynching was postponed.

Action of this sort is better for the moral health of the community than if the sheriff and the governor had permitted the mob to have had its say. There seems to be a growing respect in the south for the orderly processes of the court, and there is certainly more of a disposition there to prevent mob law than has prevailed for many years.

No state can be governed by two systems of laws—one enforced by the mob and one by the duly chosen officers of the state and governed by the acts of the legislature. So long as there are statutory provisions for the trial and punishment of criminals these laws should be recognized. If any legislature sees fit to provide that certain offenders shall be killed by mobs then such executions would become legal. As the situation stands now no state provides for lynch law. And it is well that it is so.

GOING GIVEN TWENTY YEARS.
Sent From Rome to Atlanta Under Military Escort.
Military Escort.

Rome, Ga., Oct. 14.—The jury in the case of Albert Going, colored, charged with criminally assaulting Miss Leslie Peyton, brought in a verdict of guilty this afternoon at 6 o'clock, with recommendation to the mercy of the court. Judge Henry sentenced the negro to twenty years in the penitentiary.

Going has been kept in Atlanta since the day after his arrest for fear he would be lynched. This morning he was brought to Rome under the protection of soldiers from Company B. A detachment of soldiers from Company E. of Lyndale, and the Hill City Cadets met the Atlanta troops in East Rome. Every entrance to the Court House was closely guarded, and only newspaper reporters and a few others were allowed to attend the trial.

Going was sent back to Atlanta on the 8:13 train. Miss Peyton, the girl whom it is alleged Going assaulted, is 18 years of age, and is an imbecile. She was placed on the stand and stated that the negro threatened to kill her if she did not submit to his demand. Dr. Hamilton and the girl's mother and father appeared against Going.

The conditions in the rear of the police station on King street were practically the same and it is estimated that fully 7,000 people were congregated in the two thoroughfares. Thirty policemen were on duty, and kept the crowd back. No one was allowed to enter the public passage way leading through, passing the entrance of the police station from Market to King streets.

MOB ATTEMPT RESCUE

Suspected Leader of Mob That Burned Negro at Wilmington, Arrested
NOT QUESTION OF INNOCENCE
Thousands Will Participate in Violent Interference With Any Attempt to Bring to Justice Those Participating in the Lynching.

Wilmington, Del., June 25.—At 9:30 last night a mob, ugly in temper and apparently ripe for violence, was in full possession of Market street in front of the police station and for a square or more on each side of it. In the station was confined the Indiana showman, Arthur Corwell, who was arrested on a charge of murder in having participated in the lynching of the negro murderer White on Monday night.

The rumor spread about town in the afternoon that Corwell would be taken before Coroner McCormick at the inquest to be held over the handful of charred bones which is all that is left of the negro ravisher and murderer. This it was which brought the crowd to the police station. It began to gather as early as 7 o'clock and in less than an hour was a tumultuous, threatening mob of thousands. The street in front of the station was so densely packed that street cars were brought to a standstill or made their way along at a snail's pace. The crowd swarmed into the station yard and up the steps of the building in a dense mass that pressed against the doors with a weight that seemed to threaten to crush them in. To have attempted to remove Corwell would have been sheer madness. He would have been snatched from his guard in a twinkling and borne off in triumph on the shoulders of the mon.

It was not that the mob was convinced of Corwell's innocence that it wished to rescue him. It was rather because it is believed or hoped that he had participated in the lynching. The present temper of tens of thousands of people in Wilmington points straight to violent interference, wherever such interference might be possible, with any attempt to bring to justice the leaders or participants in the lynching of the negro. The mob last night was sufficient demonstration of that fact. It included in its ranks probably one-third of the voting population of Wilmington. It represents a sentiment in the city and surrounding country that has got to be counted with.

The authorities seem to be aroused to the fact as they never have been before since the ominous threats of lynching began, as early as Monday morning last. When Corwell was arrested at first bail was refused, the charge being murder. Last night's demonstration caused a hasty modification of their attitude.

The mob made no threats. Probably a large porportion of it was made up of mere curiosity-seekers, but it was dogged and showed no signs of dispersing. On the contrary, its numbers were steadily increasing, and as time moved on its temper became more demonstrative. Negroes who appeared on its outskirts were hustled and shoved about. Spasmodic fracases broke out here and there. It took the turn of giving every street car that came along rousing cheers, because it is a generally accepted belief that it was a trolley car motorman who led the mob that burned the negro alive.

All thought of taking Corwell to the coroner's inquest was abandoned. Chief of Police Black said that it would be folly to undertake it. Meantime the coroner's inquest went on. Thomas Leech, Charles Forward, William Carter and Deputy Kilmer were the witnesses. Carter testified to having seen the negro burned, but was unable to identity of anybody concerned in burning him. Forward told about seeing the body the next morning. Leech, who is the son of the man who found the dying girl on the highway, could only testify to a visit he had made to the scene of the burning the next morning, and Deputy Kilmer's evidence merely related to getting the few scraps of charred bones on which the inquest was held and bringing them into the city the next morning.

On this testimony the coroner's jury quickly rendered a verdict that the negro had come to his death at the hands of persons unknown. The instant this verdict was rendered City Solicitor Reinhardt started for the police station, where the mob was assembled. By terrific exertion he forced his way up the station building's steps and there announced the verdict to the mob, which greeted the news with wild cheers.

This verdict gave Attorney General Ward the opportunity to do what a number of people, alarmed at the situation, were urging him to do, and that was to release Corwell on bail, which was done. Thomas McHugh, a liquor dealer, promptly became the accused's bondsman in the sum of $5,000, and he was released to appear in court this morning. Corwell, accordingly, was brought out of the police station and exhibited in plain view to the crowd, which broke out into wild yells of triumph, and at last slowly dispersed. Corwell was taken across the street to a hotel, where he remained all night.

ONLY MADE MUCH NOISE
Coroner's Jury's Verdict Did Not Implicate Corwell, and He Has Been Released on Five Thousand Dollars Bail.
(By Associated Press.)

WILMINGTON, DEL., June 24.—Arthur Corwell, who claims his home is in Hartford City, Ind., and who was arrested last night on the charge of complicity in the burning to death of George White, the negro assailant and murderer of Helen Bishop, was released on $5,000 bail tonight. He will be given a further hearing to-morrow.

Popular feeling over the tragedy of Monday night has not entirely disappeared. To-night about 2,000 persons gathered in front of the City Hall, where Corwell was confined, and made a demonstration. The police authorities took every precaution to prevent an attempt at rescuing the prisoner by the crowd. Extra police were on duty within the police station, and all the police officials were on hand in case of trouble. The crowd committed no overt act, however, beyond making a great noise. There were loud cries for the release of Corwell, to which the police paid no attention.

The coroner's inquest was concluded tonight, and when word reached the police station that the verdict did not implicate Corwell, the authorities decided to release him on $5,000 bail. This was promptly furnished by Thomas McHugh, of this city, a wholesale liquor dealer. Word of this action soon reached the crowd, and a great cheer was sent up, after which the people quickly dispersed.

The coroner's jury found that George White came to his death by a party or parties unknown to this jury.

The belief is growing here that no one will ever be punished for the work of the mob.

GREAT DISORDER.

After the crowd at the City Hall dispersed to-night scenes of lawlessness were enacted in different parts of the city, especially in the colored settlements. The entire police force was kept busy putting down disorder. In the section known as "White Chapel," a negro assaulted a white man and several whites came to the rescue. This brought reinforcements to the negroes and a general fight was started, which was stopped by the police.

While this was going on about seventy-five men gathered in front of houses occupied by colored people on Orange Street and bombarded them with bricks and other missiles. The police also quelled this disturbance.

Two Negroes Are Seriously Wounded and Two Policemen Are Injured While Clubbing the Rioters.
CORWELL TO HAVE HEARING
INDIANA MAN WHO IS CHARGED WITH BEING A LYNCHER.
Charge of Murder to Be Changed to Manslaughter—Governor Hunn Denounces the Mob.
WILMINGTON, Del., June 25.—A riot broke out in the streets late to-night between whites and negroes and for a time assumed serious proportions. The arrival of a squad of police, however, quickly dispersed the participants. Two arrests were made. A large gang of negroes, which had been marching up and down Ninth street, was challenged by about twenty-five white men, and in the fight that followed a hundred shots were exchanged.

A squad of policemen under Captain Evans and Sergeant McDermott charged the mob. The negroes and whites fled, but the police captured two negroes, Leander Moore and Joseph Shockley. The policemen used their clubs freely and in the melee attendant on the arrests McDermott and Patrolman Green received slight wounds. One negro, James Mercer, was shot in the head during the riot, but his wound is not believed to be serious.

In a brawl in another part of the city William Cramer, a negro, was shot in the stomach by a white man. He was taken to a hospital in a serious condition.

The leaders of the party of negroes who were marching in Ninth street to-night declared that they intended to resent the attacks made on members of their race last night. They say they have been abused and that they do not intend to quietly submit to such abuse. They say they have no sympathy for George F. White, the negro who was lynched for murdering Miss Helen Bishop.

Arthur Corwell, of Indiana, who was arrested in connection with the lynching, will be given a hearing to-morrow. It was the intention of the police to give him a hearing this afternoon but for some reason it was postponed. At the hearing tomorrow the charge of murder will be changed to that of manslaughter. Corwell's bond of $5,000 was renewed, Thomas McHugh, a wholesale liquor dealer, and Col. James P. McComb, a capitalist of Claymont, going bail.

In an interview to-day, Governor Hunn said: "Conditions at Wilmington are a great humiliation to the entire State. I have come here against my physician's orders to get a grasp on the situation. The way things have progressed is most serious; what has been done so far by mobs I do not think could have been prevented by the authorities, but a halt must be called instantly. After hearing of the mob's work last night in forcing the release of the prisoner, I felt that I could not stand back any longer. The fair name of Delaware has been dragged in the mire. It was no ordinary mob that released the man who murdered Miss Bishop. The crowd seems to have been composed of good citizens. The effect of their work has been disastrous. The law must now be sustained at any cost, I have not yet decided whether or not troops will be called out. I trust that will not be necessary, but the whole power of the State will be used to protect its officers in the discharge of their duties."

WILMINGTON, Del., June 26.—Col. Wickersham and Major Doherty of the First Regiment, Delaware National Guard, with a squad of men took possession of the State armory in this city to-night. Their object was to prevent a possible raid upon the armory.

A Gatling gun was stationed at the entrance and the work of burnishing arms and getting them in readiness for possible use went on until a late hour. The guard will be continued all night. Col. Wickersham said he had received no instructions from the Governor, but as custodian of the armory and its contents he deemed it best to be prepared.

The request of the Mayor that children be kept from the streets was well observed to-night. The fact that no crowd was permitted to gather had an excellent effect, and it is believed that the worst is over. There are, however, vague rumors of what may be done to-morrow night. There is a half holiday on Saturday, and the danger will be increased when the usual Saturday crowds gather. It is possible that the saloons will be closed until Monday.

Judge George Gray of the Third United States Circuit Court, it was said this afternoon, had offered to go bail for Arthur Corwell in the event of his being held for trial. When questioned on the subject he said:

"It is an occasion when the least said the better. I think it a most regrettable and deplorable occurrence, and the sooner order is restored the better it will be. I hope that our citizens will be quiet and refrain from exciting talk and anything that will continue the excitement of the past few days.

"I thoroughly indorse the views expressed by Mr. Hardy. I did not offer to furnish bail for Corwell, but if he had been held in bail I would have been as willing as other citizens would to go on his bond. That is only one of the orderly processes of the law and has no significance."

As a result of last night's riots, William Kramer, a negro, who was shot in a fracas on what is known as "the coast," a negro district, died at the Delaware Hospital at 3 o'clock this morning.

Several negroes in different parts of the city were shot, and what began as a clash between white and black men reached its climax in a fight among negroes themselves. This occurred about midnight, 100 yards from the Pennsylvania railroad station, and it was during this trouble that Kramer was shot.

William Simms, a negro, with whom Kramer had had an argument, was arrested by the police and in the City Court this morning was charged with murder and held without bail to await the action of the Coroner's jury.

Two men who were arrested during last night's rioting, Leander Moore and Joseph Shockley, both negroes, were also arraigned in the City Court this morning before Judge Cochran. Moore was charged with striking Police Sergeant McDermott on the head with the butt of a revolver. He was convicted and sentenced to one year in the county workhouse.

Shockley was accused of shooting a revolver, although he was not seen to point the weapon at anybody. He was sentenced to pay a fine of $50 and the costs of the prosecution, which will mean imprisonment if he is unable to pay.

Arthur Corwell, the only man arrested for participation in the burning of the negro White, was acquitted and released to-day after a hearing.

The hearing took place at the office of Magistrate Hollis. Corwell, who was present with his bondsman, was represented by former Congressman L. Irving Handy and former Deputy City Judge Sylvester D. Townsend, Jr. Attorney-General H. H. Ward and his deputy, Robert H. Richards looked after the interests of the State. The court room was filled to suffocation and the crowd blocked the street outside.

Detective Francis, who was the first witness, testified that he arrested Corwell as a result of a conversation between Corwell and a man of the name of Saunders as to what they saw at the burning of White, and swore that Saunders had said that Corwell was one of the men brought here to do the job. ALLEGED WHITE CAPPERS ARE BOUND OVER.
Testimony Before United States Commissioner at Troy Shows Bad Condition of Affairs in Section of Pike County.
Troy, Oct. 31.—(Special.)—Yesterday evening at 2 o'clock, the cases of Boss Riley, Will Pitman, Tumps Chesser, Robert Windham, John Windham and Fletcher Windham, charged with whitecapping, were called for preliminary hearing before Commissioner Tutwiler in this city. Assistant District Attorney Sternfeld was present to prosecute the cases.

Beside the large crowd of spectators present, there were about twenty-five or thirty witnesses for the Government, and about a dozen for the defendants. On account of the large crowd present who were anxious to learn the particulars of the cases, the Circuit Court room in the Court House was procured in which to hold the trials.

Failing to get through with the hearings yesterday, the cases were resumed this morning.

According to the evidence of the Government witnesses, rather startling conditions exist in Cross Roads and Linwood beats, about twelve miles north of the city. Negro churches were burned, negroes whipped and notified to leave the country. The house of Joe Browning was shot into and the house of a negro woman, Mary Clements, was riddled with shot and she forced to flee from her home. While running away from her house with her baby in her arms, herself and baby were shot. The shot took effect in the back of the negro woman's head and her baby was struck by shot; neither one being very seriously wounded.

The principal witnesses for the Government were: James and S. A. Daniels, Green and Henry Tate, B. P. and J. P. Floyd, C. W. and J. H. Parish, E. Golff, Clint Turner and W. C. Griffin, white men, and quite a large number of negroes.

Several notes warning and threatening negroes were introduced in evidence:

Garfield Williams, a tenant of James Daniels, received the following notice:

"Sept. 7, 1903.

"Garfield Williams, we warn you to square up your business and get out from here at once. If you owe anybody anything, pay it up and get out. And you must go twenty-five miles from here inside of five days, or death will be your portion. We intend to kill you if you stay around over five days.

"The W. C. of I. and C."

At the bottom of this notice is drawn the picture of a dagger and a heart. This notice was placed on the doorsteps of Williams. This negro is reputed to be a good farm hand and inoffensive.

Joe Browning received a notice inclosed in a miniature coffin, telling him to leave.

The whole crew of hands at Williams's mill were notified to leave the country or be killed. A number of them did leave, as well as a number of others who did not receive notices, but were frightened by the notices the others received, and the mill had to shut down. These negroes, it is said by some of the best white people of that community, are quiet inoffensive negroes.

Will Sewell, a negro farm hand, was whipped one night in April of this year so severely that the blood ran from his wounds and he was unable to work for three weeks. It was in evidence that he was whipped as a medicine and tonic. He was tied and castigated with a wagon whip.

The negro churches burned were Dunn's Chapel and Antioch.

The defendants, with the exception of one, are all young men. The other notices received by the negroes are too obscene and profane for publication.

It is said that there has been an effort made to intimidate both white and negro witnesses for the Government, and every effort on the part of the Government will be made to apprehend the guilty parties and put an end to these practices.

The witnesses for the Government are re-subpoenaed so that they can receive the protection of the Government.

The best element of the people of this county are bitterly opposed to this character of crime, as it tends to cripple the farming as well as other interests.

ELI HILSON ASSASSINATED.
Waylaid and Murdered In His Buggy, While On His Way Home From Brookhaven.
Brookhaven.

Eli Hilson, a negro living about eight miles from Brookhaven, was assassinated within about a quarter of a mile of his home Saturday evening, while on his way home from town alone in his buggy. The bullet which killed him entered the side of his head near the ear and came out at the mouth. Death seems to have been instantaneous. The horse went on home, and his owner was found dead in the buggy on his arrival.

Coroner Geo. Lambright, Jr., visited the scene of the murder Monday, impaneled a jury and held an inquest, the verdict being that the deceased came to his death by a gunshot wound at the hands of parties unknown.

Last winter Hilson, who lived on a farm of his own and was prosperous, was warned by the whitecaps to leave, which warning he disregarded. About three or four weeks ago his home was visited in the night by whitecaps and several volleys fired into it. His wife was sick in bed at the time, with an infant only a few hours old. He still disregarded the warning, and remained on his place. Saturday he brought a young daughter to town in his buggy to spend the Christmas holidays with his brother, G. N. W. Wilson, of this city, and as he was returning home between sunset and dark was assassinated. Hilson is the second negro murdered by whitecaps in that portion of Lincoln county within the last month.

From all The Leader can gather of the facts and circumstances, it is a disgraceful state of affairs and calls loudly for determined action and corrective measures by law abiding citizens and all law officers of the county. An old farmer who lives several miles below where this murder occurred, stated while in The Leader office Monday, that about all the negroes had been frightened out of his neighborhood, and that all white farmers who had more lands than they could work themselves were left without labor and that these lands will have to lie out, uncultivated.

The Leader is informed that it is the intention of the British and American Mortgage Company, which has been an extensive loaner of money on farm lands in this county, to stop all further loans and instruct its agents and trustees to foreclose all mortgages that are not promptly satisfied before the situation grows worse and the lands become less valuable.

Our local banks share this same feeling of distrust and uneasiness, and will either be forced to refuse loans in localities where this disturbance of negro labor prevails, or else demand greater security and a higher rate of interest on such loans as are advanced.

The situation is indeed a serious one to the farmers and the financial interests of the entire county, to say nothing of considerations of humanity and our boasted Christian civilization; and these dastardly white cap outrages ought to be suppressed and those who commit them hunted down and brought to justice.

The Lynching Evil. nation over retiring liberty
The Lynching Evil.

"No nation ever retains liberty after it ceases to maintain the law," writes Bishop Warren A. Candler, in his admirable and timely excoriation of the lynching evil, which The Constitution publishes today. And no nation can rightly boast of having attained a high stage of civilization whose people do not make respect for the law the corner stone of their practice, as well as of their profession. Only through respect for the law, and the determination to see it upheld in every instance and at any hazard, can that state be reached in which the rights of men are respected and perfect justice secured.

Bishop Candler uses language none too strong in criticising those who would condone the anarchy which takes the form of lynching. For it is anarchy in its most dangerous form—anarchy which does not deign to notice property, but goes after human life. The dangers he sees in the spread of the lynching evil are not overestimated. Drive from the people respect for the law, and you strike down the law; and then comes anarchy and the deluge.

There are, unquestionably, extreme provocations for lynchings in some cases, but there is no honesty in the claim—north or south—that lynching is resorted to only as summary punishment for a single crime. Take the country over and the records will show, as pointedly emphasized by Bishop Candler, that not more than one-fourth the lynchings of recent years have come as punishment for the unspeakable crime. An Indiana lynching which resulted in the killing of several people had its inception in resentment toward a criminal for shooting a policeman, a Mississippi lynching was inspired by an attempt at arson; a mob broke loose in Illinois, overthrowing the law and committing murder, because some innocent negroes attempted to work in the mines there; there have, unquestionably, been many lynchings which had no possible relationship to the crime of rape.

Everybody knows that the day has long since missed when the mob confined its lynching outbreaks to punishment for that one crime. Once that may have been the case, but it is not true now. This fact demonstrates the insidious progress this particular form of anarchy is making, and fully warrants the conclusion that unless the good people put down the mob, the mob will put down the good people.

Condone the action of lynchers in overthrowing the law and taking unto themselves the right to judge and punish for one crime, and they demand wider latitude and greater power. Tell the mob it is right in disregarding the courts and defying the sworn officers of the law in one instance, and it immediately declares itself superior to the law in all instances. If it is to be allowed to act as regulator in one thing, it sees no reason why it should not administer punishment in all things according to its own pleasure. It requires no violent stretch of the imagination to see the mob, unless properly put down, demanding as a right that it be permitted to inflict its death penalty upon a man because of his political or his religious beliefs. That has been the experience of other lands, and human nature is not greatly changed by a few years, a few decades, or even a few centuries.

This lynching mania has manifested itself in all parts of the country. Its consideration furnishes no merely local or sectional problem. It is a blot upon American civilization, a menace to the peace of the land. Instead of seeking to find excuse for it, all good people should join with Bishop Candler in condemning it and in putting down, and keeping down, the mob every time it seeks to trample the law under foot.

Lynching is no cure for any evil; it is in itself an evil that is working grave harm to our American civilization, one that must be stamped out if that civilization is to be one worthy the name.

Prompt action by the authorities, who spirited them away from the scene of the arrests, and finally landed them safely at Geneva, saved the man and woman.

There is no doubt that the angry crowd which gathered at Batavia was in earnest. Two assaults had been committed during the day by colored men and women, who attended the picnic at Mill Greek, two miles from town, given by the congregations of Quinn chapel an Bethel M. E. church, Chicago.

Mrs. George Burton, one of the most prominent women of Batavia, was set upon by two colored women and severely beaten, when she ordered a crowd from the lawn in front of her residence, where men and women were creating a disturbance.

Reaching home after a struggle, Mrs. Burton telephoned for aid, and Marshal William Kelley went to her rescue. His appearance was the signal for an attack upon him. He was knocked down and beaten by the maddened women, and kicked by the men until he was unconscious.

"He's done for," shouted one of the ringleaders when the officer gave no signs of life, and the crowd thinking him dead started on a run for the picnic grounds, two miles away.

Mrs. Burton was alone at home, but as soon as the mob disappeared, she went to Marshal Kelley and, after a time, succeeded in bringing him to his senses. He could scarcely move, but insisted upon returning to the town, a half mile away, and getting help. Mrs. Burton wanted to go instead, but the marshal feared she might meet some of the negroes on the way. She had tried in the meantime to use the telephone, but failed. The officers said Sunday night they believed the negroes had noticed the wires, which run by the carriage barn, where some of the rolsterers were, before entering the house, and had cut the connections.

Marshal Kelly reached the town hall at Batavia so exhausted that he could not speak. He was bleeding from a dozen wounds and covered with dust, for he fell from sheer weakness several times. When he was able to tell what had happened, Marshal Martin quickly gathered a few citizens and swore them in as deputies. Mounted and in carriages they drove to the Mill Creek picnic grounds, taking Marshal Kelly with them.

There were nearly 2,000 men and women at the picnic, and it seemed a hopeless task to find the fifty or more who had assaulted the marshal. The negroes made the work even harder, for as soon as Marshal Kelly had been taken past one group many of them would run ahead and mingle with the crowd in another part of the grounds. Threats were made even in the presence of the little posse to start the trouble afresh. Occasionally a melon rind would be thrown from the crowd, and missiles became even thicker when Marshal Kelly pointed out a woman as one he had seen on Mrs. Burton's lawn.

"You don't make any arrests here!" shouted a big colored man, and immediately the cry was taken up by hundreds. But just then a rescue party came on the scene.

Its appearance could not have been more dramatic if a plot had been laid out. It seems that as soon as the possee left Batavia citizens who had not been sworn in as deputies organized a party of their own and thirty men, armed with rifles and shotguns set out for the picnic grounds, arriving just when it looked ugly for the marshal and his men.

Marshal Martin had difficulty in keeping peace. The negroes, cowed and sullen, made no more hostile demonstrations, but the blood of the Batavia people was up and they wanted to find the guilty people.

A conference was held, however, which brought forth a new plan. Marshal Kelly had lost consciousness again and it was decided not to tax his strength further, and as there was no one else there who could identify the men or women who were wanted the plan of stopping the train was adopted.

The marshal, his deputies, and the volunteer possee made their way to the town and then began preparations for the next move. More deputies were sworn in, cool-headed men being picked, and a message was sent to Geneva for Robert Burke, sheriff of Kane county. The trouble had been explained to him over the telephone and he reached Batavia shortly after 5 o'clock with twenty men.

Henry Johnson Hung this Afternoon at Kaufman.

Special to Daily Light.

Kaufman, Tex, May 30, 2:30 p. m.

—Henry Johnson, the negro who criminally assaulted Mrs. John Whitworth, a young married woman, near Kemp Monday evening, expiated his crime on the gallows here this afternoon.

The hanging was public and was witnessed by several thousand people who were here from all parts of the Kaufman and adjoining counties. A special Midland train brought in a large crowd from Ennis.

The gallows were erected in the northeast corner of the court house yard. The Terrell military company was drawn up around the gallows to keep the crowd back and only three or four officers and a negro preacher were on the scaffold with the condemned man. The ceremonies on the scaffold preceding the execution were brief. The negro preacher offered a short prayer and Johnson talked about ten minutes. He was carried up on the scaffold in an arm chair and remained seated in the chair while talking. He had to be held up by officers while the black cap and noose of the rope were adjusted. Promptly at 1 o'clock Sheriff Bill Henderson cut the rope that launched the negro into eternity. The fall was sufficient to break his neck and in four minutes his body was pulseless. Ten minutes after the drop was sprung the negro was pronounced dead. The body will be interred on the county farm.

During the hanging a negro struck at one of John Whitworth's brothers with a large knife, but failed to inflict a blow. A crowd is pursuing him. He lives near Kemp and is regarded as a bad negro.

RAILROADED TO HIS DEATH. Negro Hanged Legally in Texas Four Days After Committing an Assault.
NEW ORLEANS, May 31.—Henry Johnson was hanged the "Nacogdoches way" at Kaufman, Tex., yesterday, for an assault on Mrs. Wentworth. He was hanged legally within four days of the crime. The case was so railroaded through the courts that there was no time to erect a gallows in the jail. It was impossible under these circumstances to enforce the State law, which forbids hanging in public, and thousands of persons came into Kaufman from the surrounding country and witnessed the hanging.

There was no attempt at violence. The militia, sent to Kaufman to prevent a lynching, were drawn up in the railroad yard and kept the crowd back until the body had been cut down.

The negro confessed that he committed the crime for which he paid the penalty. The law requires that a condemned man shall have thirty days of grace after the sentence of death has been pronounced, but the negro waived this and also waived any appeal to a higher court, as Mrs. Wentworth is lying at the point of death. Great difficulty was encountered in preventing a lynching and only the presence of militia stopped Judge Lynch.

The Nacogdoches way of immediately hanging after sentence of death seems popular in Texas, where it is said to prevent mobbing, rioting and lynching, and also to deter negroes from crime.

NEWS OF THE DAY.
In an address before the Lutheran Assembly at Dixon, Ill., yesterday, Judge Grossecup, of the United States Circuit Court, said that government control of monopolies is essential to the perpetuation of American institutions.

A. E. Batson was hanged at Lake Charles, La., yesterday, for the murder of the Earl family in February, 1902, near Welsh. Batson always denied the crime. The board of pardons recommended his commutation, but Governor Heard disregarded the recommendation.

The Farmers and Merchants' Bank of Montgomery, Minn., was not opened for business yesterday, and the whereabouts of the cashier, B. A. Brainerd, is unknown. The deposits run from $50,000 to $60,000 and the liabilities are estimated at $150,000. No one knows what the assets amount to.

An examination of the condition of the City Trust and Banking Company, of Baltimore for which receivers were appointed last June, shows liabilities of $675,008 and estimated assets of $250,-468. This will wipe out the entire capital stock of $100,000 and leave a stockholders' liability of over $150,000.

The alleged embezzlement of $45,000 of the funds of the Commercial Banking Company, for which E. E. Johnson, the trusted clerk of the bank, is under arrest, has brought about the failure of the Merchants' Bank of Duluth, which closed its doors yesterday. This is the fourth bank suspending business as a result of the alleged embezzlement.

Sarah Polite, colored, and two children were killed by lightning Thursday at Brogdens, in Sunter county S. C. The woman was in the act of closing a window when killed. The infant in her arms was knocked across the room and seriously injured, but is still alive. The other two children were on the opposite side of the room.

Although promised protection by officials, negroes are continuing to leave Whitesboro, Texas, in large numbers, and it seems but a question of a short time until the city will be without a colored resident. The mob, which was foiled in an effort to lynch a negro Wednesday night, warned the negroes to leave and committed many depredations in the colored section. Several negroes were severely flogged, their houses entered and furniture destroyed.

The people of the Susquehanna river town of Wrightsville, Pa., are in a state of excitement due to the action of unknown negroes who chase and try to seize and assault unprotected white women on the streets at night. During the past several nights a dozen women have thus been thoroughly frightened by negroes. Citizens are planning to apprehend the offenders and, if successful, they threaten to deal out lynch law. The situation has caused race feeling to become strong among the whites of the town.

The accommodation passenger train from Pittsburg, on the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad, due at Wheeling, W. Va., at 1:30 yesterday evening, and a freight train met in a head-on collision near the Peninsula tunnel. The engine of the freight was almost completely demolished and the front of the passenger engine smashed in. Engineer Davis, of the freight, sustained a broken leg, while the two firemen had arms broken in the jump for safety. Several passengers were considerably shaken up and bruised, but were not otherwise injured.

Mrs. Perley G. Beach, of Parkersburg, W. Va., quarreled yesterday with Miss Louilla Cain, who, Mrs. Beach says, is the object of too marked attentions from Mr. Beach. Later Mrs. Beach met Miss Cain on the street and the latter drew a revolver, which she pressed against Mrs. Beach's breast and fired. Mrs. Beach pushed the pistol away and the ball took effect in her leg. She took the revolver away from Miss Cain, removed a knife which Miss Cain had in her belt and proceeded to give her a thrashing. Warrants are out for both women.

Prof. Charles Chollette, one of the most popular members of the faculty of the West Virginia University, was found dead about a mile from Morgantown, W. Va., yesterday morning. Professor Chollette had left home in the early morning to hunt squirrels, accompanied only by his dogs. In climbing over a fence with his gun cocked a rail had broken, throwing him over the fence on his gun with such force as to cause its discharge, the shot entering the abdomen on the lower left side and causing death from hemorrhages of the main blood vessel.

NEGRO POISONING PLOT?
Texas Authorities to Investigate the Alleged Cause of a Race Riot.
NEW ORLEANS, Aug. 15.—The authorities of Grayson county, Tex., will investigate the recent race riots at Whitesboro, which resulted in driving many negroes out of the town. The mob that attacked the negroes numbered about three hundred. It is intended to arrest the leaders.

The trouble has been brewing since a negro was lynched there more than a year ago. The negroes denounced the lynching and kept the question open, with threats of what they would do. A paper was found purporting to be resolutions adopted at a negro meeting in which it was proposed to poison the wells in revenge, and when the water at the railroad station was discovered to be poisoned a belief arose that the negroes were actually plotting revenge.

This led to the race riots and the attack on the negroes. While quiet now exists in Whitesboro, it is still insisted that all negroes must leave the town just as soon as they can do so, no matter whether they have to sacrifice their property. The Grand Jury will investigate the entire affair, especially as to the paper which caused the trouble and the persons who wrote it.

Blacks Refuse to Leave Whitesboro, Tex., When Ordered, and Summary Action Follows.
REPUBLIC SPECIAL
REPUBLIC SPECIAL.

Denison Tex., Aug. 16.—In the town of Whitesboro, this county, a state of terror prevails, owing to attempted assaults on white women by negroes and the poisoning of drinking water. The citizens are wrought up to a state of frenzy.

Every negro has been ordered to leave the city under the segerest penalty. Last night seventeen negroes who had disrgarded the warning were publicly whipped.

The streets to-night are patrolled by armed white men. A great many negroes have fled. A force of United States Marshals and county officers has gone to the scene.

Lynching Frustrated.
Whitesboro, Tex, August., 13.—exodus of negroes has resulted from an attempt at lynching which was frustrated here last night. A negro named Brown, who was under arrest for attempting to assault a white woman, was hanged to a mob to a tree, but was rescued by the Sheriff and posse.

The negro was unconscious when rescued and the Sheriff arrived just in time to save him. The mob believing they had accomplished their purpose retired as the Sheriff and posse approached. In the meantime the negroes were so terrorized that they began to leave, fearing that the mob, having been prevented from killing Brown, would attack them generally as there is much feeling among white people.

A negro attacked a white woman about a week ago and that night a negro accused of the offense was hanged by a mob, but rescued and saved from death by the sheriff and a posse.

SLEEPER TO RUN THROUGH

No Change of Cars From Chicago to the Coast.

BY ASSOCIATED PRESS.

Chicago, Aug. 20.—As a result of the merger of the Northern Pacific, Great Northern and Burlington railroads, a through sleeper is to be inaugurated to coast points, doing away with the necessity of changing cars in St. Paul and Minneapolis.

A late night train to Chicago, connecting with Pacific coast trains, will be added soon, it is said.

The matter was decided on by President Hill of the Great Northern and President Harrison and Vice-President Miller of the Burlington.

The terrible storm which swept over the West Indies last week seems to have wrought the greatest havoc on the Islands of Jamaica and Martinique. At Port Antonio on the north coast of Jamaica, only six houses were left standing. Vessels were blown from their moorings and dashed to pieces at sea, while wharves and store houses were completely demolished. On the island of Jamaica hundreds of lives were lost, and it is said the property loss will exceed ten millions. The storm was equally severe in the eastern and western ends of the island.

Dr. Frankenfield, an attache of the weather bureau at Washington, in a special report on the floods of the Missouri valley which created such havoc recently, places the property loss in excess of $7,000,000. The report, when completed in every detail, will be transmitted to congress. It will include estimates of the cost of the erection of flood gauges at different point along the Missouri and its tributaries and the expense of sending the special information gathered from them to the headquarters of the bureau in Washington. It will be the design to show that if the government had been able to maintain a few river observers along the tributaries and the channel of the Missouri ample warning could have been given to the people so that they could not only have reached places of safety themselves, but removed their stock and bulky household goods also.

Taylor Has Malmed Many Family Pets in His Efforts to Obtain Fees, and Is to Be Further Prosecuted.
New Rochelle in addition to its colony of the allied trades, consisting of artists, actors, humorists millionaires, playwrigths, yachtsmen and plain commuters, now boasts of a dog catcher whose delight is to pick off the bounding fox terrrier or the household toy spaniel with a shotgun. For indulging in his favorite pastime to-day he was fined $3 for discharging a shotgun and held to await trial on a charge of cruelty to animals.

Mr. Peel is the poundkeeper, marshal and general head of the dog-catching industry of the city. For an assistant he has James Taylor, a negro. Taylor is the man behind the gun and may possibly become the man behind the bars. It is Taylor's business to drive a latticed cart and get from the wagon every few minutes and place a copper wire about the neck of a stray cur or the blooded pup of some one of the best families of the city from whose neck the collar has been stolen.

But the chase, the getting on and off wagons for the last few weeks, has been too great and the wagon is becoming known, so Taylor has been carrying a gun. The residents assert that when in the pursuit of his legal fee for getting a dog Taylor would rather take him dead than alive, and the crack of the shotgun has been heard from Lather's Hill and the Paine monument as far east as the fort erected by Francis Wilson. Every time it has been heard some pet of a family has fallen either dead, mortally wounded or maimed for life. Having got his victim the negro, it is said, hurls the dog into the wagon and goes off in search of another.

For weeks the dwellers of the Hill and Residence Park have been afraid of stray buckshot and in fear that fudo will become the next victim. To-day the negro was caught red-handed taking a pot-shot at a fox terrier. The shot carried away a leg of the dog and in a few minutes the negro with his gun was surrounded by a crowd who shouted "Lynch him" in the most approved Delaware tones.

A policeman, the one on the regular force of the city, was called, and he arrested Taylor. The negro's defense was that he had first caught the dog with a wire and that after that it escaped from him, and so he took a shot at it. For the shooting he was fined $3.

Harry Stiles, a prominent young man of New Rochelle, who was in court, then made a charge of cruelty to animals against Taylor, and upon this charge the Poundkeeper's assistant will be prosecuted by Officer O'Brien, of the S. P. C. A. In the meanwhile the allied trades of art, literature and money in New Rochelle are hoping the negro will be sent away until the dog days are over.

George Hobough, of West Point, Probably Fatally Wounded There.
WAS DANGER OF LYNCHING
Negro Taken to King William Jail and Wounded Man Brought to the Virginia Hospital.
As a result of the murderous assault by a negro at West Point Saturday evening, George Hobough, a small truck farmer of King William county, now lies at the Virginia Hospital desperately wounded and with the chances of recovery strongly against him, while John Clements, the negro who shot him, is a prisoner in the King William county jail, after a thrilling escape from violence at the hands of the infuriated citizens of West Point and vicinity. The cool judgment of influential citizens prevented summary justice being visited on the negro for his deliberate and persistent attempt to murder Hobough. As it was, he was conveyed to the county jail and there safely incarcerated, to await a fate almost as certain as that which he escaped Saturday night, for if his victim die he will almost certainly be convicted of murder, with the extreme penalty.

INSULTED BY CLEMENTS.

Among those who saw the shooting, which now portends a tragedy, was Captain C. W. Westour, of this city, district passenger agent of the Southern Railway, who had gone to West Point Saturday night to spend the Suhday. Hobough, it seems, came to town with his wagon on business, and while on the street he was jostled and insulted by Clements, a Baltimore negro, who had been employed in West Point for some time as an oyster shucker. He demonstrated with the negro, but the latter became offensive and Mr. Hobough knocked the negro down while the latter was attempting to get at a knife. While Hobough had the negro down a crowd of other negroes gathered around and were about to come to the aid of the negro. At this juncture Mr. Pitcher, who keeps a butcher shop near the scene of the encounter, seeing the situation, rushed out and warned the negroes that if they attempted to lay hands on Hobough he would use the cleaver he had with him upon the first one who made a demonstration. Clements was let up and allowed to go away.

Hobough completed his purchases, and when starting down the street to his wagon he was warned by Mr. Pilcher that he had better not go alone, but Hobough insisted that he was not afraid of the negro, and departed.

SHOT HIM DOWN.

It was then dark and Hobough had not proceeded far before he encountered the negro coming toward him and armed with a revolver. Being himself unarmed, he turned around and started back down Seventh Street with the negro in pursuit of him and close behind him, attempting at every step to shoot him. The revolver snapped and missed fire several times when the negro was in two or three feet of his victim. Finally after several attempts, the weapon was discharged and the negro kept on shooting. Mr. Hobough exhausted by his run and his wound, for one bullet had taken effect, ran into a doorway to escape his murderer pursuer and fell just inside. While he was laying prostrate within the doorway the negro again shot him this time in the hip.

A crowd of negroes who had watched the pursuit and the crime, then called to Clements to run, and he did so. A posse of citizens quickly formed and sent out armed with shot guns in every direction in which the negro might escape from the point between the two rivers on which the town is situated. Two of them hurried up the railway in the direction of this city, hoping to intercept the fugitive. As they were running in the darkness they met a negro who asked them for a match or as to the time, and one of the two men hunting the negro, happening to know him, recognized his voice and covering him with a gun, informed him that he was under arrest.

MADE NO STATEMENT.

"That is for the court to decide."
He would make no further statement.

SUCCUMBS TO HIS INJURIES
West Point Dairyman, Shot by Negro, Dies at the Virginia Hospital.
After lingering nearly two weeks, George Hobough, the West Point dalryman, who was shot on the night of December 12th by the negro, John Clements, died at 11:30 o'clock yesterday morning in the Virginia Hospital in this city.

There is some question of the direct cause of the death of the injured man. I tappears, however, that the pneumonia, with which he was suffering during the latter days of his illness, devolved first in the lung penetrated by the negro's bullet, and afterward extended to the sound lung, which would make it appear that the death is directly the outcome of the wounds. Whether or not an inquest will be held is a matter that will be determined to-day upon the arrival of the Commonwelath's attorney of West Point. Arrangements for the funeral will also then be made.

Shortly after he was advised of his critical condition, Hobough made an ante-mortem statement to Detective Captain Tomlinson. The grand jury, at noon, convened in special session by Judge Rasch, returned an indictment for murder against the negro Lee, also known as Lee Brown, who murdered Patrolman Massey on Friday night. A rumor was started that Lee would be returned to the city this evening for trial, and great excitement followed the announcement. Preparations were made at once to have an organized body of armed men meet all incoming trains this evening for the purpose of searching every car in the hope of finding Lee. Judge Rasch made the positive announcement that Lee will not be returned to the city at this time.

Many negroes went into hiding and scores of others are leaving the city. Help in homes and hotels was very scarce. The negroes are badly frightened.

Otherwise the city was quiet during the day. There were few signs of the violence that agitated the population all of last night. Business is moving along in the even tenor of its way. A trip in the business section revealed the fact that much damage was done to numerous stores, especially to the hardware stores, many of which were entered and robbed of guns and ammunition. Thousands of shots were fired during the night, but so far as learned no one was killed, although several persons are said to have been wounded. Several negroes were caught by mobs and almost beaten to death before the police could save them.

After the mob last night was thoroughly satisfied that Lee, the murderer of Patrolman Massey, was not in the jail, it separated into squads of forty or fifty and paraded the downtown streets until daylight, shooting promiscuously and visiting the negro quarters.

The local companies of the State militia were ordered out and will be reinforced by companies from southern Indiana.

The funeral of the murdered patrolman, held this afternoon, was the first influence to give a decided impetus to the inflamed sentiment that culminated in to-night's disaster.

Wallace's circus, which showed here today, declared off the evening performance and loaded on trains and departed early in the evening.

In that part of the city nearest Baptisttown, the negro settlement, white residents are in a frame of mind bordering on frenzy, it having been reported that the negroes intended to burn the houses and shoot the inhabitants. Policemen and deputies were sent there to guard lives and property. Colored ministers visited the mayor and offered to do all they could to hold in check the lawless colored element.

Several hundred deputy sheriffs and policemen were sworn in and armed this evening. Every policeman is carrying a Winchester rifle or other gun and each patrolman is in charge of a squad of deputies patrolling sections of the city. The day has been filled with rumors and replete excitement. Governor Durbin has been urged by the authorities and prominent citizens to order State troops to the city, but the only ones on duty are the local militia. It was rumored that the Governor had ordered five companies of soldiers to this city, but later he denied the report. He feels that the local authorities have not exhausted all power at their command.

But few negroes were to be found around their usual haunts in the afternoon and early evening, and it was feared they were awaiting an opportunity to make an attack. The mayor issued a proclamation ordering all the saloons closed at 6 o'clock, and warning all citizens to remain at their homes and in that manner assist the authorities.

About 9 o'clock to-night a mob of about a thousand persons gathered about the jail. Most of the members were evidently drawn there by curiosity, but a number of the leaders of last night's disorders were in evidence, and, as the situation showed threatening signs, it was turned over to the military. Cordons of troops were thrown around the jail, and pickets posted in the streets converging at that point. All the local commands are on duty, and the companies from several other Southern Indiana towns are on their way here to reinforce the local contingent. The mob was scattered for the time being, but the streets leading to the jail were rallying points for a number of detached bands.

When the mob first gathered, at about 9 o'clock, it was held in check by the militia, but there was nevertheless great disorder, and this increased with the accession of numbers. A young man named Jaegler was stabbed with a bayonet by a soldier, but was not dangerously wounded.

Frank B. Posey made a speech to the people, urging them to disperse. He reassured the crowd that no good could come from such demonstrations, and that the negro murderer, Robert Lee, had not been brought back to the city, as had been reported. Several incendiary speeches were made by men who were prominent in last night's disorder. Demands were again made that a committee be allowed to search the jail, as was done last night, but Sheriff Kratz refused to allow this. But for the presence of the militia it is believed the jail would again have been stormed. There was much talk about making another visit to Baptisttown and driving the negro population away.

Country roads were strewn with them during the day. Men had to be detailed from other houses to fill their places. Steamboats that have had trouble for weeks to secure colored deckhands were overrun to-day with applications for work. THE RACE WAR IN INDIANA.
WISCONSIN
WEEKLY
Advocate
DEVOTED TO THE INTERESTS OF THE NEGRO RACE

VOLUME V.

Mob Law Must Be Put Down.

New York Post: "Race War in Indiana" is now a familiar headline. But the news from Evansville, in that state, represents a condition of affairs which is nothing less than anarchy. All last night the city was terrorized by mobs of whites armed with the loot of gun shops, seeking the lives of every Negro and bent on blowing up all the dwellings in the colored quarter. The reason for this fresh outbreak of savagery in an American city is simply rage at failure to lynch a Negro who three days ago killed a policeman, but who was spirited away in time to save him from lawless hanging or even burning. No white woman figures in this case as in the Wilmington shame. The excuse of the "one crime" therefore fails again, as it has failed innumerable times, to account for white savagery. But matters have seemingly come to such a pass that lynch law must prevail whatever a Negro's crime, and no matter how many additional lives must be sacrificed in such an orgy of passion and of vengeance. There are some more sinister features in the Evansville outbreak than in any thus far reported to bring discredit to our national honor—arming of the blacks as well as whites, the riddling with bullets of Negro's homes, and the sharp lining up of one race against another. What is to come of it, if some authority can not soon be found to vindicate the law, to punish mobs, and to make clear the terrible guilt of every participant in the shame of such outrages in whatever town or state?

RACE DIFFICULTIES
The killing of Policeman Massey of Evansville, Ind., by a Negro named Lee Brown has caused no end of trouble in that city and in that part of the State. Owing to the threats of a mob gathered at the jail Lee was hustled off to Vincennes for safety. A rumor was started that he was to be returned after an indictment by the grand jury, in consequence of which a mob again gathered about the Evansville jail with the view of making short work of the prisoner. The militia was called out to disperse the unlawful gathering, but the mob considered it merely a bluff, and after a time grew bold, insulting the soldiers and in many ways showed contempt for them. It got to a point where the taints could no longer be borne. They were ordered to fire, which they did with disastrous effect; six dead and twenty-five wounded being the result. The autocraties from Governor Durbin down have exercised the utmost vigilance in trying to preserve the State against the disgrace of mob violence which, as the Governor states, is uncalled for. Justice was sure and swift for the criminal, Lee Brown, who offended doubly in shooting down an officer of the law. The act was atrocious, but not beyond the acts of other men. The anti-Negro spirit was beyond it all, a spirit which the State cannot afford to encourage since it would weaken the force of all law, as it concerns Negroes, who make up a considerable portion of the State's population, and also white men who may not happen to be in favor. It goes without saying that the Negroes deplore the crime of Lee Brown and take no pleasure in the awful slaughter that subsequently took place among the people of the city of Evansville. We are safe in saying that they feel more keenly the great loss of life and regret more sincerely the awful happening than the whites owing to the awful possibilities hanging on the event. GREENCASTLE, Ind., May 17.—One of the most puzzling crimes that has ever been committed in this county was the murder of Mrs. Henry Seward in her home a mile and a half west of Fern station, last evening.

With her head crushed by blows from a club, lying in a pool of blood by the side of a bed in her front room, Mrs. Seward was found by her husband when he returned in the evening from his work on the farm. The couple had been married less than a year and had just gone to housekeeping on their own farm. Mr. Seward was alarmed when he neared the house by the lack of signs of his wife's presence, and he quickly went through the rooms till he found her.

There was no sign of robbery having been committed in the house, or of criminal assault, and the motive for the awful deed cannot be found. The murderer is thought to be a negro tramp who was noticed climbing on a freight train on the Big Four Railroad, going west, about 4:45 that evening. It was 6 o'clock when the woman's body was found. She evidently had been dead about an hour and a half.

Her body lay by the bed, in the front room of the farmhouse. She evidently had been taking an afternoon nap on it when she was disturbed. She had removed the fancy pillow cases and the bed itself was pressed in as if by the weight of her body. When found she was on her face, with one foot under the edge of the bed. One ear was split open, her cheek was cut to the bone, one side of her lower jaw was broken, and on the back of the head, at the base of the skull, was found the mark of the fatal blow. The skull had been crushed in and death had probably been instantaneous after it was inflicted. The blows were confined to her head. On one side of her neck a small piece of skin had been flicked out, but below her neck there was not a mark of violence.

Freight trains coming eastward toward this city were searched by officers and tramps were taken off and put in jail, but there was no indication that any of them had known of the crime.

The excitement in the neighborhood in which the murder was committed was intense and had any negro been found on a freight train and taken back to Fern, his life undoubtedly would have been a thing of small value.

GREENCASTLE, Ind., May 18.—Within the last few hours public sentiment has thoroughly shifted in regard to the identity of the murderer of Mrs. Henry Seward, two miles west of Fern, this county. When her husband reported the finding of her body, some time after 6 o'clock Saturday evening, it was remembered that a negro tramp had been seen climbing on a freight train near the house about an hour and a half before the report of the murder was started by Seward, and it was presumed by the neighbors, and suggested by Seward, that the negro had been the murderer, but other circumstances have developed since that time, and there is a probability that Henry Seward will be placed under arrest within a few hours. He and a neighbor had been at work in a cornfield less than two miles from the house and went part of the way home together, having left the field at 5 o'clock. Seward could have reached his home within half an hour from the time he left the field, had he walked at an ordinary gait, it is said. He did not report the finding of his wife's body until after 6 o'clock.

The club that was used to kill her had been cut from a six-foot hickory pole that had been lying a hundred feet from the house in a hollow. It was taken to the woodyard, a few yards from the house, where the club was cut from it with an ax, the fresh chips being found by the officers. There must have been considerable noise in connection with the chopping of the pole. The club was found after the report of the crime, near the railroad, a hundred yards from the house. lena-lena-1903-05-17.A15:
CRIME STILL A MYSTERY
MURDER OF MRS. SEWARD, IN PUTNAM, UNCLEARED BY INQUEST.
Husband Cleared of Suspicion—Stabbing Affrays at Muncie and Terre Haute—Publican Indicted.
Special to the Indianapolis Journal. GREENCASTLE. Ind. May 20
GREENCASTLE, Ind., May 20.—The coroner's investigation of the murder of Mrs. Henry Seward in her farm home last Saturday evening failed to bring out evidence which would incriminate her husband in the killing, nor was there evidence of any strength against any one in particular. The original supposition that the murder was committed by a tramp is being given more credence to-day and the position of the husband is becoming better as a result.

The principal points that were urged against him were that he was a long time in going from the field, two miles from the house, in which he was plowing, to the house and in giving the warning of the murder afterwards, but there have developed witnesses whose testimony shows that the time occupied by Seward was not at all longer than was necessary. There was also a report that he changed his clothing after reaching the house, before giving the alarm, and that the overalls he wore when he went to the house could not be found, but the officers who went to the place yesterday evening found them where he said he had put them after changing. He said he had not changed them until after 10 o'clock that night.

The coroner's examination was private, but it is understood that no new point was developed, at least that is what is said by some of the witnesses, and none of the witnesses made new statements when they were interviewed by the press to-day.

lena-lena-1903-05-17.A24:
PARALLELED IN A NOVEL
CRIME FOR WHICH HENRY SEWARD IS HELD AT GREENCASTLE.
Book Found in Alleged Murderer's Home-Mrs. Drake Released on Bond-Attempt at Suicide.
Special to the Indianapolis Journal.
GREENCASTLE, Ind., July 15.—The crime of the murder of Mrs. Henry Seward, for which her husband is now in jail, is claimed by many people to be a duplicate, intentionally, of one outlined in a detective story found in Seward's home. The most striking similarity is in the following passage in the story, coming immediately after the finding of the body of the victim:

"The surgeon who was summoned declared that the death had been the result of a crime, that the wounds and fractures on the head and face had been caused by some heavy instrument, such as a hammer; that from the position of the body Gabriel Boysson must have been assassinated in bed."

A detective in the story investigates the murder and describes the method used in the killing as follows:

"The unfortunate man slept. Then the guest, armed with a mallet or hammer, entered; he advanced to the bed and satisfied himself that his host was asleep; he raised the weapon and struck the first blow on the forehead; Boysson was only stunned; he arose, and without seeing, extended his arm and caught his assailant with his hand."

The story is "Victor Maurey," but the name of the author cannot be found. Surgeons who were consulted about the injuries on the head of Mrs. Seward say they could not have been inflicted with the bloody club that was found; that a hammer or some instrument of that nature must have been used. Mrs. Seward was also first struck as she lay on her bed asleep, and she arose after the first blow, only to be struck down again, this time to the floor.
lena-lena-1903-05-17.A27:
SEWARD MURDER HEARING.
Not Much of Importance Developed Against the Suspect.
Against the Suspect.
Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

GREENCASTLE, Ind., July 28.—The first day of the preliminary hearing of Henry Seward on the charge of the murder of his wife closed without the introduction of evidence that convinced the justice before whom it was held of the guilt of the defendant. The testimony of only three witnesses was completed and the case will be taken up again in the morning. One witness testified that Seward had objected to his wife going to her father's to help there and had said in that connection, "If she does not quit it I will bump her."

Another said Seward had told him when told that the officers had seemingly begun working on other suspects than himself, "Perhaps I have switched them." The same witness testified that Seward said, "Just because I killed my wife," and then changed his statement to, "Just because they think I killed my wife they are afraid of me."

Dr. J. M. King, coroner, testified that death was caused by blows from a club or other blunt instrument and stated that a hammer could not have done it, in his opinion.

The justice said he would not hold the prisoner on the evidence introduced so far. The case will be continued to-morrow.

Fired into the House.
Fired into the House. Memphis, Tenn., Sept. 23.—A posse which went with bloodhounds in pursuit of a negro who fired on M. V. Vlum, a white citizen of Shelby, Miss., was led by the dogs to the house of M. Carter. When the men knocked on the door for admission, the lights were put out. They then broke down the door, while the negro emptied his pistol without hurting anyone. The posse replied, fatally wounding Carter. He is now in jail in Shelby, and should he show signs of recovery, he will undoubtedly be lynched.

Negro Wounded and Captured After Firing On a Posse Near Shel- By, Mississippi.
Shelby, Miss., Sept. 24.—The posse with bloodhounds in pursuit of the negro who fired on M. V. Blum, a white man, Monday, was led straight to the house of M. Carter, two miles from here. When the men rapped for admittance the lights were extinguished and as they broke down the door the negro fired twice, but hit no one. The posse replied, fatally wounding Carter. He was brought here and should he show signs of recovering will be lynched.

FOUGHT RUNNING BATTLE WITH NEGRO BURGLARS. Citizens Headed Off Fugitives, Who Were Escaping on Handcar, and Battle Followed.
REPUBLIC SPECIAL.

Danville, Ill., Oct. 5.—Excursionists returning home early this morning surprised three negro burglars in the store of William Lynch at Muncie, eight miles east of here. The burglars jumped on a Big Four handcar and pumped west.

Citizens of Oakwood were informed by telephone and Village Clerk Robert S. Pinager organized a posse, placed a heavy plank, secured by a crowbar, on the track and then hid in the bushes.

The handcar soon came up at top speed, struck the obstruction and went into the air about four feet. The three burglars were not hurt and began running as the posse opened fire.

A running battle followed, during which many shots were exchanged. The robbers finally outran their pursuers, and disappeared in the darkness. One of the possemen was grazed by a bullet and it is believed one or more of the burglars were struck by small shot.
oakwood-oakwood-1903-10-07.A3:
NEGRO BURGLARS GET WORST OF IT
Citizens Returning Home at Danville Find and Route Housebreakers.
Danville, Ill., Oct. 7.—A lively battle between three negro burglars and a posse of citizens occurred at Oakwood, twelve miles east of here. Returning excursionists surprised and routed the burglars, who were plundering William Lynch's store at Muncie. They escaped on a Big Four hand car, going west. A message was sent to Oakwood, and Town Clerk R. S. Pinnegar organized a posse of twelve, placed a plank, held in place by a crowbar, on the track, and hid in the bushes.

The burglars evidently expected resistance, and approached the town at top speed. When they struck the obstruction the car was thrown into the air and the men were pitched headlong to the ground. The posse opened fire, and a running fight through the village followed. The burglars finally disappeared in the darkness. One of the posse was slightly injured, a bullet grazing his arm. Officers have failed to get track of the robbers.

SAVED FROM LYNCHING BY A MASONIC SIGN
Colored Preacher in Texas Proved He Was Member and Was Rescued.
DALLAS, Texas, March 12.—The Rev. D. R. Stokes, the most prominent negro preacher and educator in Dallas, has given to United States Marshal W. H. Atwell the facts of an attempt to lynch him in Gregg county on the night of February 25, and his rescue by one of the most prominent white men of that county, who had been one of the foremost in demanding that he be lynched.

Mr. Stokes states that he had been hired to make speeches against prohibition, and had been campaigning vigorously among the negroes. While he was making a speech a large body of white men rushed into the meeting, seized him, took him to the Sabine River, rowed him to the other side, and prepared to hang him.

In his desperation the minister made the sign of distress of the Masonic order. One of the white leaders instantly stepped to his side and demanded that the negro's life be spared. He refused to give his associates his reasons for his change of mind, but simply said: "Spare him and I will guarantee that he never again sets foot in Gregg county."

The crowd finally consented and the white Mason hurried Mr. Stokes out of the county. The minister has not been there since and says he never intends to go there again.

United States Attorney Atwell has investigated Mr. Stokes' story and found it true.
