Turned Over to United States Navy Department by President.
Washington, March 18.—The president by executive order has turned the Midway islands over to the navy department. This was done at the instance of the Pacific Cable company, which has asked for the protection of its properties on the islands. Roving Japanese sailors are in the habit of putting into the islands for the plumage of sea fowl and for guano. It is probable that the navy will establish a small station on the islands and American warships will make a practice of touching there much more frequently than they have done in the past. The islands are two in number—Sand island, having 633 acres, and Eastern island, 245 acres. There is a harbor affording about eighteen feet of water. The islands are deemed essential to the operation of the Pacific cable which will touch there on its western route from Hawaii.

The Arrest.
Special to Times-Republican.
Muscatine, Aug. 13.—Bert Sheppard, the son of a wealthy coal operator of Oskaloosa, (Iowa) was arrested in Muscatine yesterday charged with the murder of Arthur Meade, the young West Liberty man who was shot and instantly kiled in a restaurant in his home town on the night of May 14.

The information upon which Sheppard was arrested was furnished by Sheriff Andrew Hofer, of Iowa City, Johnson county, and Night Police MacBurnett, of the same city, the latter claiming that to the best of his belief Sheppard answers the description of the man given by those who saw the supposed murderer on the night of the tragedy.

The arrest of Sheppard is the culmination of a line of work that was started by Officer Mac Burnett four weeks ago.

"On the night preceding the murder of Arthur Meade," said Mr. Burnett, "a dozen or more men climbed off the blind baggage of train 41 on the main line in Iowa City. I immediately rounded them up and sent for the patrol wagon. One load of the men were taken to the station, and the wagon returned for the remainder. In the remaining bunch there were two men who particularly attracted my attention. They appeared to be very much disappointed over being taken to the station and insisted that they had to reach Des Moines by the following morning.

"I noticed them carefully. I observed how they were dressed, particularly one of them, and since the murder of Arthur Meade, I have gone over the case until I am almost positive that one of the men answers the description of the man given by those who saw the murder committed. We have been trying to locate this man for quite a while and it was only a few days ago that we traced him to Muscatine."

Sheriff Hofer, and Officer Burnett arrived in Muscatine at 8:10 o'clock this morning, and immediately after breakfast began the search for their man. The arrest of Sheppard was hastened by the fact that Chief Rice and Officer McElravy had just taken the man wanted to the city jail.

This morning before the arrest was made Sheriff Hofer said:

"I believe that the man we want stands a better show of getting away now than he will after we get him."

Bert Sheppard, who is a young man about 22 years of age, denies emphatically that he knows anything of the murder of Arthur Meade, and states that his arrest is all a terrible mistake.

"I have been in Muscatine for a week or ten days, said Sheppard to a reporter in the county jail, 'and I came down here to visit a friend. I was in Davenport the other day, and a friend of mine who lives in Muscatine, remarked that when I got ready to go home to come by way of Muscatine, and remain here for a few days. I did so, and when arrested, had no idea of what was wanted with me.

"I don't want any notoriety out of this thing," he said, "and I wish you would keep it out of the papers. In Oskaloosa my people are as good as can be found anywhere, and if this affair was to happen there, I would have no trouble in getting out of it and getting out quickly."

Sheppard is a handsome fellow about twenty-two years of age. After his arrest he appeared to be rather nervous but he told a story that conflicted in no particular.

"I have never been in Wilton in my life," he said, "and I don't even know where the town of Nichols is. About four years ago I was in West Liberty, but have never been in the town since that time.

"I have no fear over the outcome of this affair, and I am sure that when the two men who they say will be asked to identify me, arrive, they will agree that the wrong man has been arrested."

No Evidence Against Man Accused of Killing Arthur Meade.
Muscatine, August 14.—Bert Sheppard, the young Oskaloosa man arrested Wednesday on the charge of the murder of Arthur Meade at West Liberty May 14th, was acquitted yesterday in his preliminary hearing and fifteen minutes later a negro, Tom Clay, who was largely responsible for his arrest, was ordered to leave Muscatine by the first train.

Clay, who was just released from the Johnson county jail, where he served a sentence for crushing a man's skull, led Sheriff Hoffer and Officer Mac Burnett to believe that the man who had been seen by them was in Muscatine.

Coming here Wednesday he pointed out Sheppard. He also claimed to have other evidence at hand. Accordingly Sheppard was arrested. Following the Oskaloosa man's release the indignation against Clay was so intense County Attorney Ingham, Sheriff Sweart and Justice Eversmeyer called him up and gave him until the next train to leave town. There were several other remarks exchanged and finally the negroes started over with the announced intention of "wiping out the white element."

Kevil, the scene of the miniature race war night before last, will probably hereafter, if reports are true, become a second Calvert City, where colored people are not allowed to stop over night. Since the shooting in which Crockett Childress, a white youth, was badly, if not fatally shot Sunday night and the white people who happened to be around were forced to seek cover to escape flying bullets, there has been a great deal of feeling among the residents of that section of Ballard, as well as across in McCracken county.

Yesterday, according to reports, quite a number of people came to the city and invested in guns and pistols, and every man in the locality of the imbroglio was a walking arsenal before night.

Trouble was in the air, and the colored people got scent of it. They began leaving yesterday moring in twos and threes, according to reports, and by night there were none to be found. There were doubtless a few left, but they contrived to keep pretty close.

It was generally expected that there would be "something doing" after dark, and a number of Paducah people received invitations to go out and witness the fireworks, but they declined.

WAITES M'CAA WAS KILLED BY A NEGRO
He Reprimanded Will Jones and a Fight Ensued
NEGRO NOT YET CAUGHT
The Tragedy Occurred in Brewer & Jones Commissary at Trussville. McCaa's Remains Were Brought to Birmingham.
Details of the murder of Waites G. McCaa, at Trussville Tuesday afternoon, reached Birmingham yesterday morning when the remains arrived. The killing was done by Will Jones, a negro, and occurred at the commissary of Brewer & Jones, contractors for the Seaboard Air Line railroad.

The negro struck McCaa three times on the head with an axe, two of the blows crushing his skull and causing almost instant death. The dead man and his brother, B. B. McCaa, both shot at the negro, and it is believed that two of the bullets took effect. The negro cried out as if in pain and was traced for a long distance by a trail of blood.

Searching for Negro.

Coroner Paris went to Trussville yesterday morning and with deputy sheriffs and armed citizens made a search for the negro, but at a late hour last night they had not been able to find him. It is fear that the negro will be killed should he be caught.

The trouble between McCaa and the negro started over the former ordering the latter to saddle his horse so he could ride to the camps of the firm. McCaa was employed as paymaster, while the negro worked around the commissary.
Negro Impudent.

The negro was rather slow in saddling the horse and was impudent to McCaa. Finally after the saddle was on the horse McCaa told the negro to go into the commissary and get a hickory switch which was hanging in there. The negro walked away in a sulky manner and remained in the place longer than he should. When he came out he had a small hickory which was useless and McCaa reprimanded him for this and his past behavior.

The negro became angry and cursed McCaa for some time, until the latter reached for his pistol and started for the negro. Instead of shooting him at once, McCaa began beating him on the head with it. The negro proved to be the stronger and they wrestled for some time. the negro finally breaking away and securing the pistol.

At this juncture McCaa grappled with him again and his younger brother secured another pistol and fired at the negro five times.

He went back to the commissary to re-load the pistol and when he returned he found his brother dying. He was leaning against the wall in the feed room and there were two large holes in his head from which the blood was pouring. The negro had escaped.

On the floor near where the dead man was lying was found the pistol over which he and the negro had fought. There were two chambers which had been discharged and it is thought that McCaa fired them at the negro during the fight. Still nearer the body was the bloody axe with which the murder had been committed.

Death From the Blows.

It was at first thought by the younger McCaa that his brother had been shot by the negro, but an investigation yesterday morning at Warner-Smiley's undertaking establishment by Dr. Mack Rogers showed beyond a doubt that death was caused by blows from a blunt instrument and not from bullets. There are a number of gashes and bruises on the body of McCaa, showing what a desperate fight there had been between he and the negro. His arms were gashed and bruised and it is supposed that was caused by his attempting to ward off the blows of the negro. There is a powder burn on his right arm near the elbow.

It is not known whether this came from the pistol of the younger McCaa when he fired at close quarters, or whether the deceased was holding the pistol close to his arm when he fired at the negro in the struggle.

The remains were brought into Birmingham yesterday morning in a wagon. They were not placed on the Alabama Great Southern train Tuesday night because it was late, and it was thought time could be saved by hauling the body through the country. The remains were carried to Warner-Smiley's establishment.

The services will be conducted from the residence this morning at 10 o'clock and the interment will be in Elm Leaf cemetery. The family lives on Fourteenth street between Ninth and Tenth avenues, south.

Troy, Sept. 11.—(Special.)—Considerable excitement has been created in Cross Roads Beat in the upper portion of this county by whitecappers. For some time there has been manifestations of hostility toward the negroes in that locality which has resulted in two or three personal conflicts.

Some time ago a negro named Browning was notified to leave the community, and on his failure to do so, his house was shot into at night. Monday night of this week a notice in writing was placed on the house of a farm tenant of J. M. Daniels, ordering him to leave, which frightened the negro, and he left. James Phenix, who is doing a small mercantile business at Linwood, about twelve miles north from this city on the Central of Georgia Railroad, operates a four or five horse farm in the edge of Cross Roads Beat, and a night or two ago his negro tenants were given notice to leave, and all except one or two have left him.

R. J. Williams (who is foreman of the grand jury now in session here), together with his son, Lon Williams, owns and operates a steam saw mill in Cross Roads Beat, and their employees are mostly negroes. These negroes were notified by the whitecappers to leave and they did so. Lon Williams and the negroes are in the city today.
As soon as the Sheriff heard of the trouble he went to the locality, and he and a deputy worked there all day yesterday trying to obtain clues as to the guilty parties. The Sheriff returned to the city today, leaving his deputy to look after the matter. The Sheriff brought with him several of the notices that had been posted warning the negroes to leave. These notices gave the negroes five and ten days to leave the country, threatening them with shooting and death on their failure to do so. The notices contained the most obscene and indecent epithets, and most of them were signed, "Negro Skinner," and some were signed "W. C. J. and C." The grand jury is in session, and the most rigid investigation into this affair will doubtless be had, two members of the grand jury having had their employes frightened away from their employment by this lawless element.

The defendants are: Boss Riley, Robert Windham, Temps. Chesser, Fletcher Windham, John Windham and William Pittman, well known white farmers residing about twelve miles from Troy.

These men are accused of a grave offense. It is alleged that they have repeatedly served notice on negroes to leave the county; that they whipped five or six negroes severely; that they are members of an organized gang which burned two negro churches; shot a negro woman and her baby and fired a shot gun into the house of a negro.

The six men were arrested Tuesday by Deputy Marshal J. F. Green who took them to Troy where they were admitted to temporary bail of $500 each by Commissioner Tutwiler who set their cases for trial Friday.

Government agents have been actively engaged in securing evidence in the whitecapping cases. A number of letters said to have been written Pike County negroes are on file in the office of the United States District Attorney. These letters are crudely written and some of them are filled with profanity and vulgarity. All of them demand that the negroes leave the county. They are signed "Negro Skinners," "Negro Killers," or with initials. One letter bears a heart and dagger, crudely drawn.

It is said that when the United States grand jury meets in Montgomery in December a number of whitecapping cases will be drawn to its attention. At least six of these cases will come from Barbour County.

HELD TO GRAND JURY

Testimony Before United States Commissioner at Troy Shows Bad Condition of Affairs in Section of Pike County.
Troy, Oct. 31.—(Special.)—Yesterday evening at 2 o'clock, the cases of Boss Riley, Will Pitman, Tumps Chesser, Robert Windham, John Windham and Fletcher Windham, charged with whitecapping, were called for preliminary hearing before Commissioner Tutwiler in this city. Assistant District Attorney Sternfeld was present to prosecute the cases.

Beside the large crowd of spectators present, there were about twenty-five or thirty witnesses for the Government, and about a dozen for the defendants. On account of the large crowd present who were anxious to learn the particulars of the cases, the Circuit Court room in the Court House was procured in which to hold the trials.

Failing to get through with the hearings yesterday, the cases were resumed this morning.

According to the evidence of the Government witnesses, rather startling conditions exist in Cross Roads and Linwood beats, about twelve miles north of the city. Negro churches were burned, negroes whipped and notified to leave the country. The house of Joe Browning was shot into and the house of a negro woman, Mary Clements, was riddled with shot and she forced to flee from her home. While running away from her house with her baby in her arms, herself and baby were shot. The shot took effect in the back of the negro woman's head and her baby was struck by shot; neither one being very seriously wounded.

The principal witnesses for the Government were: James and S. A. Daniels, Green and Henry Tate, B. P. and J. P. Floyd, C. W. and J. H. Parish, E. Golff, Clint Turner and W. C. Griffin, white men, and quite a large number of negroes.

Several notes warning and threatening negroes were introduced in evidence:

Garfield Williams, a tenant of James Daniels, received the following notice:

"Sept. 7, 1903.

"Garfield Williams, we warn you to square up your business and get out from here at once. If you owe anybody anything, pay it up and get out. And you must go twenty-five miles from here inside of five days, or death will be your portion. We intend to kill you if you stay around over five days.

"The W. C. of I. and C."

At the bottom of this notice is drawn the picture of a dagger and a heart. This notice was placed on the doorsteps of Williams. This negro is reputed to be a good farm hand and inoffensive.

Joe Browning received a notice inclosed in a miniature coffin, telling him to leave.

The whole crew of hands at Williams's mill were notified to leave the country or be killed. A number of them did leave, as well as a number of others who did not receive notices, but were frightened by the notices the others received, and the mill had to shut down. These negroes, it is said by some of the best white people of that community, are quiet inoffensive negroes.

Will Sewell, a negro farm hand, was whipped one night in April of this year so severely that the blood ran from his wounds and he was unable to work for three weeks. It was in evidence that he was whipped as a medicine and tonic. He was tied and castigated with a wagon whip.

The negro churches burned were Dunn's Chapel and Antioch.

The defendants, with the exception of one, are all young men. The other notices received by the negroes are too obscene and profane for publication.

It is said that there has been an effort made to intimidate both white and negro witnesses for the Government, and every effort on the part of the Government will be made to apprehend the guilty parties and put an end to these practices.

The witnesses for the Government are re-subpoenaed so that they can receive the protection of the Government.

The best element of the people of this county are bitterly opposed to this character of crime, as it tends to cripple the farming as well as other interests.

After argument of counsel for the Government and defendants the court held all of the defendants except Robert Windham, who was discharged. Fletcher Windham was held to bail in the sum of $750, and the others in the sum of $500 each, to await the action of the Federal grand jury which convenes in Montgomery next December.
